title: Designs for Learning: Studying Science Museum Exhibits That Do More Than Entertain

findings.antecedent: Bike Cycle exhibit (complex machine work schema, immediately recognizable robot, four large, color-coded buttons)
findings.consequent: visitor persistence until success
findings.mechanism: Familiar schema reduces cognitive load, allowing focus on challenge.
findings.quote: 73% of visitors persisted until they had succeeded, and 70% said they thought the level of challenge was about right.

findings.antecedent: Downhill Race exhibit (competition/race schema, two lanes, six disks with varying features)
findings.consequent: visitor predictions, explanations, and new understandings
findings.mechanism: Familiar schema (race) provides context, freeing cognitive resources for scientific inquiry.
findings.quote: several studies have shown that this exhibit provokes predictions, explanations, and new understandings that can be articulated

findings.antecedent: Frogs exhibit (watching and waiting schema, tank with hidden nocturnal frogs)
findings.consequent: complex inferences from visitors (theories about camouflage, froggy lifestyle)
findings.mechanism: Familiar schema (waiting/watching for reward) reduces frustration, allowing for deeper cognitive engagement and social interaction.
findings.quote: most likely of any in the exhibition to elicit complex inferences from visitors

findings.antecedent: Frogs exhibit (watching and waiting schema, tank with hidden nocturnal frogs)
findings.consequent: stories, personal associations, declarations of previous knowledge
findings.mechanism: The exhibit's design, despite hidden frogs, allowed visitors to engage in social meaning-making and knowledge sharing.
findings.quote: second most likely element to evoke stories and personal associations, and the second most likely to elicit declarations of previous knowledge

findings.antecedent: Frogs exhibit (watching and waiting schema, tank with hidden nocturnal frogs)
findings.consequent: visitor frustration or annoyance
findings.mechanism: The 'watching and waiting' schema set appropriate expectations, preventing frustration.
findings.quote: None of the 30 pairs of visitors expressed frustration or annoyance at having to look for the frogs

findings.antecedent: Detective puzzle schema (framing the Whodunit exhibition)
findings.consequent: immediate apprehension of purpose and relationship of distinct elements
findings.mechanism: Familiar schema provides a clear framework, reducing cognitive load.
findings.quote: allowed visitors to immediately apprehend the purpose and relationship of distinct elements

findings.antecedent: Highly interactive (changeable lighting, focus, dish location) and live specimens OR Less interactive (changeable lighting, focus) and live specimens
findings.consequent: visitor holding time, exhibit enjoyability rating, reconstruction of relevant details
findings.mechanism: Live specimens and interactivity enhance engagement and memory.
findings.quote: visitors who saw one of the live, interactive versions of the exhibit stayed longer, rated the exhibit as more enjoyable, and were able to reconstruct more relevant details of their experience, than the noninteractive version

findings.antecedent: More interactive version (changeable lighting, focus, dish location, live specimens) vs. Less interactive version (changeable lighting, focus, live specimens)
findings.consequent: visitor experience (engagement, learning)
findings.mechanism: Adding more interactivity beyond a certain point does not necessarily improve experience or learning.
findings.quote: we found no significant differences between the experiences of visitors who used the more interactive version and those who used the less interactive version.

findings.antecedent: Display of seven optical illusions (low physical interactivity)
findings.consequent: visitor stopping behavior (stopping at all seven illusions)
findings.mechanism: Intriguing visual phenomena can sustain attention even without physical interaction.
findings.quote: a display of seven optical illusions at which more visitors stopped at all seven than stopped at any one

findings.antecedent: Exhibits with live animals in glass terrariums (low physical interactivity) vs. Physically interactive exhibits
findings.consequent: attractiveness, frequency and diversity of 'learning-talk'
findings.mechanism: Live animals, even without direct interaction, can be highly engaging and promote social learning.
findings.quote: exhibits containing live animals in glass terrariums were more attractive and evoked significantly more frequent and more diverse “learning-talk”... than the physically interactive exhibits.

findings.antecedent: Videotape of frogs catching and eating prey (non-interactive)
findings.consequent: diversity of learning-talk, longest holding times
findings.mechanism: Compelling visual content, even if non-interactive, can be highly engaging and stimulate discussion.
findings.quote: The single exhibit in the exhibition that evoked the greatest diversity of learning-talk (as well as the longest holding times) was a videotape of frogs catching and eating their prey.

findings.antecedent: APE exhibits
findings.consequent: visitor engagement duration (holding time)
findings.mechanism: APE design supports deeper cognitive and physical engagement.
findings.quote: APE exhibits engaged visitors for more than twice as long as traditional exhibits.

findings.antecedent: APE exhibits
findings.consequent: variety of 'driving questions'
findings.mechanism: APE design encourages diverse forms of inquiry.
findings.quote: elicited a broader variety of “driving questions,” defined as the initial thought that visitors had as they approached the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: APE exhibits
findings.consequent: variety in physical interaction patterns/sequences, later label reference, self-generated explorations
findings.mechanism: APE design supports more open-ended, self-directed inquiry.
findings.quote: visitors' physical interactions with APE exhibits varied in both pattern and sequence more than with the traditional exhibits, and labels were often referred to later in the sequence of exhibit use

findings.antecedent: Wooden disks designed to heighten salience of mass distribution (in Downhill Race exhibit)
findings.consequent: visitors figuring out correct principle
findings.mechanism: Making the key variable more salient helps visitors identify the correct principle.
findings.quote: When the exhibit was used with wooden disks specially designed to heighten the salience of the key variable of mass distribution, more visitors succeeded in figuring out the correct principle behind the disks' behavior.

findings.antecedent: Wooden disks designed to heighten salience of mass distribution (in Downhill Race exhibit)
findings.consequent: overall holding time
findings.mechanism: Making the principle too obvious might reduce the challenge and intrinsic motivation for deeper engagement.
findings.quote: the overall holding time decreased, and fewer visitors who could read the principle in the label engaged deeply with the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: Wooden disks designed to heighten salience of mass distribution (in Downhill Race exhibit)
findings.consequent: deep engagement with exhibit
findings.mechanism: Making the principle too obvious might reduce the challenge and intrinsic motivation for deeper engagement.
findings.quote: the overall holding time decreased, and fewer visitors who could read the principle in the label engaged deeply with the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: Traditional exhibit label (containing invitation to interact and then explanation of underlying principle)
findings.consequent: visitors articulating correct principle
findings.mechanism: Providing direct explanations helps visitors articulate the scientific principle.
findings.quote: A more traditional exhibit label... resulted in more visitors articulating the correct principle

findings.antecedent: Traditional exhibit label (containing invitation to interact and then explanation of underlying principle)
findings.consequent: deep engagement with exhibit
findings.mechanism: Providing direct explanations might reduce the need for active inquiry and deep engagement.
findings.quote: but led them to be less deeply engaged with the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: Simple partitions around a group of related exhibits
findings.consequent: percentage of visitors correctly identifying common theme
findings.mechanism: Partitions reduce distraction and visually group related exhibits, aiding conceptual coherence.
findings.quote: increased the percentage of visitors who correctly identified their common theme from 30 to 51%

findings.antecedent: New Seeing collection (designed for eye/brain function, cultural effects on seeing) vs. Original Optics collection
findings.consequent: visitor talk about seeing as interpretation, mention of visual system parts, appreciation of attention, realization of different perceptions, connection to daily lives
findings.mechanism: The new design successfully communicated subtle and complex scientific ideas by focusing on interpretation and relevance.
findings.quote: significantly more visitors to Seeing talked about seeing as interpretation, mentioned specific parts of the visual system, said they had a new appreciation of the importance of attention in seeing, said they hadn't realized that people see things differently, and found that the exhibits related to their daily lives.

findings.antecedent: Traits of Life collection (displaying diverse living creatures to illustrate commonalities)
findings.consequent: communication of abstract theme (four common characteristics)
findings.mechanism: Visitors interpreted the display as diversity rather than commonality, possibly due to existing conceptual schemes.
findings.quote: our Traits of Life collection was less successful in communicating its abstract theme

findings.antecedent: Temporary exhibition (general)
findings.consequent: explicit connections made among exhibits by visitors
findings.mechanism: Visitors may not expect or have the cognitive resources to make explicit connections between exhibits in an open environment.
findings.quote: visitors made explicit connections among exhibits at only 5% of the exhibits at which they stopped.

findings.antecedent: Exhibit collections with diverse learning styles (quieter, carpeted, selective lighting, partitions, observation/reflection support)
findings.consequent: visitor noticing and valuing diversity of spaces
findings.mechanism: Providing varied environments caters to diverse learning preferences and reduces fatigue.
findings.quote: Evaluation studies have shown that our visitors notice and value the diversity of such spaces within the museum

findings.antecedent: Inquiry video clips (asking short questions for further exploration)
findings.consequent: visitor preference, integration of exhibit experience into prior knowledge
findings.mechanism: Inquiry-based prompts are more effective than personal narratives for integrating science content in this context.
findings.quote: inquiry videos were preferred by visitors, and helped them integrate the exhibit experience into their prior knowledge

findings.antecedent: Narrative video clips (personal story about connection to exhibit)
findings.consequent: impact on learning/integration
findings.mechanism: Personal narratives showed little or no impact compared to control for integrating science content.
findings.quote: while narratives showed little or no impact compared with the control condition.

findings.antecedent: Narrative video (unfolding drama with young children)
findings.consequent: evoking personal connections in visitors' lives
findings.mechanism: Specific narrative forms (drama with children) can be more effective at creating personal connections.
findings.quote: this showed some evidence of evoking personal connections in more visitors' lives than the control or inquiry conditions.

stimuli.description: Water Standing on Air exhibit (plexiglass cylinder, metal mesh, water)
Touch the Spring exhibit (concave mirror creating image of a spring)
Bike Cycle exhibit (robotic simulation of bicycle rider with hydraulic pistons and buttons)
Downhill Race exhibit (inclined plane, two lanes, six disks of varying shape/weight)
Frogs exhibit (circular, galvanized iron tank with mini-ecosystem, hidden nocturnal frogs)
Whodunit exhibition (crime scene, DNA lab, simulated autopsy laboratory)
Glowing Worms exhibit (microscopic organisms on video screens, with live specimens and changeable lighting/focus/dish location)
Energy from Death exhibit (glass case with animals in various stages of decomposition)
Videotape of frogs catching and eating prey
Seeing Collection (exhibits on eye/brain function and cultural effects on seeing)
Traits of Life collection (exhibits displaying diverse living creatures to illustrate commonalities)
Inquiry video clips (short questions for further exploration of exhibits)
Narrative video clips (personal stories about connection to exhibits)
Narrative video (unfolding drama with young children)

limitations: Need more research on the impacts of apprehendability versus challenge, and how the tension plays out at different scales, times, and audiences.
Designing exhibits to maximize visitor-directed inquiry may sometimes decrease the chances that visitors will understand a specific scientific principle.
The field badly needs more studies of nonverbal forms of learning, especially for children, as these may be dominant forms for three-dimensional physical interaction.
Large-scale design issues for conceptual coherence are logistically difficult and expensive to test in real museum settings.
More research is needed to determine if narrative instantiations were flawed or if the chaotic, high-energy science museum environment makes storytelling an ineffective learning strategy.

Challenges for narrative include: noisy/chaotic environment not conducive to sitting/listening, upper limit of a few minutes on narrative length, visitor preference for concrete over metaphorical content, and attentional conflicts with group conversations.
